newsitem.title: TURKEY: IMF team to end Turkey assessment trip this week.
newsitem.headline: IMF team to end Turkey assessment trip this week.

text.p: A team from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will leave Turkey this weekend after a two-week trip to examine the troubled economy and the country's 1997 economic targets, Turkish officials said on Thursday.
"They will complete their study this weekend. They may leave a note on their assesment of the economy and suggestions before leaving," said a senior economy official, who declined to be named.
He denied reports in the Turkish media that the team would cut short its visit due to negative attitudes of the Islamist-led coalition government of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.
The team held talks with economy bureaucrats and government officials in Turkey.
Officials said Turkey will later signal whether the government seeks to reach an accord with the IMF.
Turkey and the IMF will begin talks for a new stand-by arrangement if Ankara shows it is ready to take measures in line with the Fund's reccomendations.
"What the IMF is to recommend will not be surprising for us. It is likely to repeat its previous recommendations," the official said.

In its reports in May and August, the IMF urged Turkey to implement a medium-term stabilisation programme including three major elements -- a fiscal tightening, structural reforms and measures designed to break "inflationary inertia and entrenched inflationary expectations."

It says Turkey should limit its budget deficit to a level which can be financed by privatisation proceeds and net foreign borrowing to enable the county to cut its domestic borowing and lower high real interest rates.

To do this, Turkey must speed up its sluggish privatisation programme, tighten expenditures and raise more tax, particularly through new arrangements in the value-added tax and corporate income tax areas, whose yield the IMF says is currently relatively low.

Turkey should also adopt the Fund's reccomendations to improve tax and customs administrations and reform the loss-making social security system to reach an accord with the IMF after its failure to complete a 1994 stand-by arrangement.
Bankers said Turkey, which expects a record high current account deficit of around $7 billion this year, needs IMF support to borrow easily in international financial markets.

However, they still cautioned that Erbakan's Welfare Party, which had appeared as the leading opponent of any deal with the IMF, World Bank and the Euopean Union in the past five years, may tend to block the way towards a deal.

The government, which announced its 1997 economic and budgetary targets last week, said it would raise some $8.5 billion through the sale of state assets, including a minority stake worth $3.5 billion in Turk Telekom.

Officials said the IMF may urge Turkey for a fiscal adjustment programme to attain budgetary targets in the first nine months of 1997 as the sale of Turk telecom shares is unlikely to be realised before the final quarter of 1997.
"They may seek Turkey to enlist a realistic revenue-raising mechanism and concrete measures to take expenditures under discipline," the official said.
Erbakan's two revenue-raising packages, unveiled in the past three months, and a zero-deficit 1997 budget draft have failed to win admiration of economists who say they are unrealistic.
The budget, based on a projection of a sharp rise in non-tax revenues, will be debated at parliament by end-1996.
Turkish industrialists said the 765-percent rise foreseen in non-tax revenues is unrealistic.

Mesut Yilmaz, leader of the opposition Motherland Party, predicted the 1997 budget deficit at 2,200 trillion lira. The 1996 deficit is expected to overshoot to 1,300 trillion lira against an initial target of 861 trillion.
